units.sourceHTML: 6 Regular expressions ¶

units.text: Regular expressions are patterns used in selecting text. For example, the ⟦0⟧ command
units.sourceHTML: Regular expressions are patterns used in selecting text. For example, the ed command

units.text: prints all lines containing ⟦0⟧. Regular expressions are also used by the ‘⟦1⟧’ command for selecting old text to be replaced with new text.
units.sourceHTML: prints all lines containing string. Regular expressions are also used by the ‘s’ command for selecting old text to be replaced with new text.

units.text: In addition to specifying string literals, regular expressions can represent classes of strings. Strings thus represented are said to be matched by the corresponding regular expression. If it is possible for a regular expression to match several strings in a line, then the left-most match is the one selected. If the regular expression permits a variable number of matching characters, the longest sequence starting at that point is matched.
units.sourceHTML: In addition to specifying string literals, regular expressions can represent classes of strings. Strings thus represented are said to be matched by the corresponding regular expression. If it is possible for a regular expression to match several strings in a line, then the left-most match is the one selected. If the regular expression permits a variable number of matching characters, the longest sequence starting at that point is matched.

units.text: An empty regular expression is equivalent to the last regular expression processed. Therefore ‘⟦0⟧’ replaces ⟦1⟧ with ⟦2⟧. Note that if a regular expression is used inside the ⟦3⟧ of a global command, the "last regular expression processed" may differ between the first and subsequent executions of the ⟦4⟧. See ⟦5⟧global command⟦6⟧.
units.sourceHTML: An empty regular expression is equivalent to the last regular expression processed. Therefore ‘/re/s//replacement/’ replaces re with replacement. Note that if a regular expression is used inside the command-list of a global command, the "last regular expression processed" may differ between the first and subsequent executions of the command-list. See global command.

units.text: As a GNU extension, a regular expression /⟦0⟧/ may be followed by the suffix ‘⟦1⟧’ which makes ⟦2⟧ match ⟦3⟧ in a case-insensitive manner. Note that the suffix is evaluated when the regular expression is compiled, thus it is invalid to specify it together with the empty regular expression.
units.sourceHTML: As a GNU extension, a regular expression /re/ may be followed by the suffix ‘I’ which makes ed match re in a case-insensitive manner. Note that the suffix is evaluated when the regular expression is compiled, thus it is invalid to specify it together with the empty regular expression.

units.text: Any character ⟦0⟧ not listed below, including ‘⟦1⟧’, ‘⟦2⟧’, ‘⟦3⟧’, ‘⟦4⟧’, ‘⟦5⟧’, and ‘⟦6⟧’, matches itself.
units.sourceHTML: Any character c not listed below, including ‘{’, ‘}’, ‘(’, ‘)’, ‘<’, and ‘>’, matches itself.
Any backslash-escaped character c, other than ‘{’, ‘}’, ‘(’, ‘)’, ‘<’, ‘>’, ‘b’, ‘B’, ‘w’, ‘W’, ‘+’, and ‘?’, matches itself.

units.text: Matches any single character.
units.sourceHTML: Matches any single character.

units.text: Matches any single character in ⟦0⟧. To include a ‘⟦1⟧’ in ⟦2⟧, it must be the first character. A range of characters may be specified by separating the end characters of the range with a ‘⟦3⟧’, e.g., ‘⟦4⟧’ specifies the lower case characters. The following literal expressions can also be used in ⟦5⟧ to specify sets of characters:
units.sourceHTML: Matches any single character in char-class. To include a ‘]’ in char-class, it must be the first character. A range of characters may be specified by separating the end characters of the range with a ‘-’, e.g., ‘a-z’ specifies the lower case characters. The following literal expressions can also be used in char-class to specify sets of characters:

units.text: If ‘⟦0⟧’ appears as the first or last character of ⟦1⟧, then it matches itself. All other characters in ⟦2⟧ match themselves.
units.sourceHTML: If ‘-’ appears as the first or last character of char-class, then it matches itself. All other characters in char-class match themselves.

units.text: Matches any single character, other than newline, not in ⟦0⟧. ⟦1⟧ is defined as above.
units.sourceHTML: Matches any single character, other than newline, not in char-class. char-class is defined as above.

units.text: If ‘⟦0⟧’ is the first character of a regular expression, then it anchors the regular expression to the beginning of a line. Otherwise, it matches itself.
units.sourceHTML: If ‘^’ is the first character of a regular expression, then it anchors the regular expression to the beginning of a line. Otherwise, it matches itself.

units.text: If ‘⟦0⟧’ is the last character of a regular expression, it anchors the regular expression to the end of a line. Otherwise, it matches itself.
units.sourceHTML: If ‘$’ is the last character of a regular expression, it anchors the regular expression to the end of a line. Otherwise, it matches itself.

units.text: Defines a (possibly empty) subexpression ⟦0⟧. Subexpressions may be nested. A subsequent backreference of the form ‘⟦1⟧’, where ⟦2⟧ is a number in the range [1,9], expands to the text matched by the ⟦3⟧th subexpression. For example, the regular expression ‘⟦4⟧’ matches the string ‘⟦5⟧’, but not ‘⟦6⟧’. Subexpressions are ordered relative to their left delimiter.
units.sourceHTML: Defines a (possibly empty) subexpression re. Subexpressions may be nested. A subsequent backreference of the form ‘\n’, where n is a number in the range [1,9], expands to the text matched by the nth subexpression. For example, the regular expression ‘\(a.c\)\1’ matches the string ‘abcabc’, but not ‘abcadc’. Subexpressions are ordered relative to their left delimiter.

units.text: Matches zero or more repetitions of the regular expression immediately preceding it. The regular expression can be either a single character regular expression or a subexpression. If ‘⟦0⟧’ is the first character of a regular expression or subexpression, then it matches itself. The ‘⟦1⟧’ operator sometimes yields unexpected results. For example, the regular expression ‘⟦2⟧’ matches the beginning of the string ‘⟦3⟧’, as opposed to the substring ‘⟦4⟧’, since an empty string is the only left-most match.
units.sourceHTML: Matches zero or more repetitions of the regular expression immediately preceding it. The regular expression can be either a single character regular expression or a subexpression. If ‘*’ is the first character of a regular expression or subexpression, then it matches itself. The ‘*’ operator sometimes yields unexpected results. For example, the regular expression ‘b*’ matches the beginning of the string ‘abbb’, as opposed to the substring ‘bbb’, since an empty string is the only left-most match.

units.text: Matches the single character regular expression or subexpression immediately preceding it at least ⟦0⟧ and at most ⟦1⟧ times. If ⟦2⟧ is omitted, then it matches at least ⟦3⟧ times. If the comma is also omitted, then it matches exactly ⟦4⟧ times. If any of these forms occurs first in a regular expression or subexpression, then it is interpreted literally (i.e., the regular expression ‘⟦5⟧’ matches the string ‘⟦6⟧’, and so on).
units.sourceHTML: Matches the single character regular expression or subexpression immediately preceding it at least n and at most m times. If m is omitted, then it matches at least n times. If the comma is also omitted, then it matches exactly n times. If any of these forms occurs first in a regular expression or subexpression, then it is interpreted literally (i.e., the regular expression ‘\{2\}’ matches the string ‘{2}’, and so on).

units.text: The following extensions to basic regular expression operators are preceded by a backslash ‘⟦0⟧’ to distinguish them from traditional ⟦1⟧ syntax. They may be unavailable depending on the particular regex implementation in your system.
units.sourceHTML: The following extensions to basic regular expression operators are preceded by a backslash ‘\’ to distinguish them from traditional ed syntax. They may be unavailable depending on the particular regex implementation in your system.

units.text: Anchors the single character regular expression or subexpression immediately following it to the beginning (in the case of ‘⟦0⟧’) or ending (in the case of ‘⟦1⟧’) of a ⟦2⟧word⟦3⟧, i.e., in ASCII, a maximal string of alphanumeric characters, including the underscore (_).
units.sourceHTML: Anchors the single character regular expression or subexpression immediately following it to the beginning (in the case of ‘\<’) or ending (in the case of ‘\>’) of a word, i.e., in ASCII, a maximal string of alphanumeric characters, including the underscore (_).

units.text: Unconditionally matches the beginning ‘⟦0⟧’ or ending ‘⟦1⟧’ of a line.
units.sourceHTML: Unconditionally matches the beginning ‘\`’ or ending ‘\'’ of a line.

units.text: Optionally matches the single character regular expression or subexpression immediately preceding it. For example, the regular expression ‘⟦0⟧’ matches the strings ‘⟦1⟧’, ‘⟦2⟧’ and ‘⟦3⟧’. If ‘⟦4⟧’ occurs at the beginning of a regular expressions or subexpression, then it matches a literal ‘⟦5⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: Optionally matches the single character regular expression or subexpression immediately preceding it. For example, the regular expression ‘a[bd]\?c’ matches the strings ‘abc’, ‘adc’ and ‘ac’. If ‘\?’ occurs at the beginning of a regular expressions or subexpression, then it matches a literal ‘?’.

units.text: Matches the single character regular expression or subexpression immediately preceding it one or more times. So the regular expression ‘⟦0⟧’ is shorthand for ‘⟦1⟧’. If ‘⟦2⟧’ occurs at the beginning of a regular expression or subexpression, then it matches a literal ‘⟦3⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: Matches the single character regular expression or subexpression immediately preceding it one or more times. So the regular expression ‘a\+’ is shorthand for ‘aa*’. If ‘\+’ occurs at the beginning of a regular expression or subexpression, then it matches a literal ‘+’.

units.text: Matches the beginning or ending (empty string) of a word. Thus the regular expression ‘⟦0⟧’ is equivalent to ‘⟦1⟧’. However, ‘⟦2⟧’ is a valid regular expression whereas ‘⟦3⟧’ is not.
units.sourceHTML: Matches the beginning or ending (empty string) of a word. Thus the regular expression ‘\bhello\b’ is equivalent to ‘\<hello\>’. However, ‘\b\b’ is a valid regular expression whereas ‘\<\>’ is not.

units.text: Matches (an empty string) inside a word.
units.sourceHTML: Matches (an empty string) inside a word.

units.text: Matches any word-constituent character (letters, digits, and the underscore).
units.sourceHTML: Matches any word-constituent character (letters, digits, and the underscore).

units.text: Matches any character that is not a word-constituent.
units.sourceHTML: Matches any character that is not a word-constituent.
